e.t: Abimelech is a proper name used for a person, rendered “Abimelech” in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies several figures in the biblical record rather than describing a quality, action, or general object. The name occurs 83 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 77 verses, with many occurrences in Judges and Genesis. Because it is a personal name, its precise referent depends on the passage in which it appears.

Hangaios, also rendered Anggeos, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies the prophet Haggai. This name appears six times, once in Ezra and five times in Haggai, including references to the prophet’s messages and recorded identity. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its normal function is simply to name Haggai.

This word means “marketplace,” referring to a public place where people gather for buying, selling, and exchange. It is a noun describing the market itself rather than an action or a person. In the Greek Old Testament and related books represented by this LXX entity, it occurs nine times, including passages in Ecclesiastes, Ezekiel, 2 Maccabees, and Song of Songs. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains a marketplace or commercial gathering place.

“Azariou; Azariu” is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal designation rather than as a description, action, or general concept. This name appears eight times across eight verses in the LXX corpus, including Kings, Chronicles, and Ezra. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide verse text or a further definition, its specific reference must be determined from the surrounding passage in each occurrence.

This verb means “proved accurate; reliable.” It describes something shown to be trustworthy or dependable, rather than merely claimed to be correct. As a verb, it expresses the action or result of demonstrating accuracy and reliability. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 46:15. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what was shown to be reliable in that passage.

This verb means “fish”: to catch or seek fish. It describes the action of fishing rather than a person, place, or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 16:16. The word’s basic meaning is clear, while its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. This LXX word should remain distinct from similarly rendered words in other biblical language corpora.

This noun means “spring” or “leap”—a sudden, energetic jump or bound. It describes vigorous movement rather than a general journey or ordinary step. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Job 39:25, so its precise force there belongs to the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea remains a forceful movement forward or upward, expressing the action of something that springs or leaps with strength.

This noun means “error” or “fault”—a mistake, failing, or wrong action. It names something a person has done incorrectly rather than describing the person as a whole. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears only once, in 3 Maccabees 2:19, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central sense remains a recognized failing or error for which a person may be held responsible.

This verb means “straighten up”—to raise, restore, or make something stand upright. It describes bringing something into a proper or upright position rather than leaving it bent, fallen, or disordered. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 16 times, including passages in Samuel, Chronicles, Psalms, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what or whom the action concerns, but its central picture remains that of lifting or setting upright.

This Greek LXX verb means “discharge; deliver.” It describes releasing someone from an obligation, condition, or danger, or sending someone away free. Its precise force depends on the sentence in which it appears, but the central idea is removal from what binds or threatens. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages from Exodus, 1 Samuel, Job, Wisdom, and the Maccabean books.

This adjective describes something left unhewn or unwrought—that is, not shaped, cut, or finished by working it with tools. It is used four times in the Greek Old Testament represented by the Septuagint, all in 1 Kings. The word can describe material in its unfinished state, before human craftsmanship gives it a prepared or fashioned form. Its basic emphasis is on what has not been worked or shaped.

This noun means a “portion,” referring to one part or share of something larger. It identifies an allotted section rather than the whole, focusing on what belongs as one part of a greater amount. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 45:20. Its precise significance there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense remains a portion or allotted part.

This verb means “leap off from”: it describes moving suddenly away from a person, place, or position. In the Greek LXX, it appears four times, each in a different verse, including Proverbs, Ezekiel, Hosea, and Nahum. Its central idea is departure expressed as a jump or spring rather than a quiet change of location. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the word itself emphasizes the act of springing away from something.

This verb means “blind” or “make blind”: it describes causing someone to lose sight or become unable to see. As an action word, it focuses on blindness being caused or present rather than naming a person, object, or condition. In the Greek Septuagint material represented here, it occurs twice, once in Wisdom and once in Sirach. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on the resulting blindness or the action that brings it about.

Ariokh is a proper name, rendered as “Ariōch” or “Ariokh.” It identifies a person rather than expressing a general action, quality, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs four times: twice in Genesis and twice in Daniel. The name appears in Genesis 14 and Daniel 2, but the available lexical information does not establish an additional meaning beyond the personal name itself.

This adverb means “newly” or “just,” pointing to something that has happened only recently or has just become the case. It describes the timing of an action or situation rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 15:34. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls more naturally on something recent or on something that has just occurred.

This noun means “star,” referring to a visible heavenly body. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for individual stars or stars considered together as a multitude. The word appears 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages that speak of the stars in the heavens. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: a star is one of the lights seen in the night sky. The surrounding context determines whether the word is being used simply for stars or in a comparison involving them.

This adjective describes something that cannot be corrupted, spoiled, or brought to an end. Its central sense is “incorruptible” or “imperishable,” pointing to lasting integrity and endurance rather than temporary existence. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in the book of Wisdom. The surrounding verse text is needed to show exactly what the word describes in each passage, but its basic meaning remains something enduring and not subject to decay or corruption.

This verb means to reign—to rule as a king or other governing ruler. It describes the exercise of royal authority, whether referring to one ruler or to a succession of rulers. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it is used broadly in accounts of kings and kingdoms, including historical records of who ruled and how long. The word occurs 371 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, so its central idea is firmly established as ruling in a royal capacity.

This noun means “assistance” or “help”—support given to someone in need. It refers broadly to aid rather than to a particular kind of person, action, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, in Wisdom and 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains clear even when the surrounding verse determines who provides the help or what need is being met.

This Greek particle means “for.” It commonly introduces a reason, explanation, or supporting statement, linking what follows with what has just been said. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it appears 1,411 times, so readers may encounter it in many kinds of sentences. Its exact force depends on the surrounding words, but its basic role is to connect an explanation or reason to the preceding statement.

Gesiri, also rendered Yesiri, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. It identifies a named person, group, or place in the Greek Old Testament, though the available information does not specify which. The name occurs five times in four verses, chiefly in Joshua and once in 1 Samuel. Its precise referent must therefore be determined from the surrounding passage where it appears.

Debba, also rendered Thevva, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It does not function as a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but identifies a named subject in the text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Joshua 21:28. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific referent cannot be described more precisely here; the supported lexical meaning is simply the name “Debba” or “Thevva.”

This word means “prisoner”: a person held in confinement or under restraint. It can function as a noun describing such a person, and its normal sense centers on being bound, detained, or unable to act freely. In the LXX corpus, it occurs nine times, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains someone held captive or imprisoned.

This word means a “ford,” a place where people can cross a river or stream, usually because the water is shallow enough to pass through. As a noun in the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a crossing point rather than the act of crossing itself. It occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages associated with Genesis, Joshua, and Judges. The word may refer to one ford or to several fords, depending on the sentence. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

“Warm through” is a verb describing the act of making something warm throughout or causing warmth to pass through it. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, so it is an uncommon word. Its basic sense is physical and straightforward: something becomes thoroughly warm rather than merely touched by heat. The surrounding passage determines what is being warmed in any particular occurrence.

This verb means “whistle,” describing the act of producing a clear, sharp sound with the mouth. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 3:50. Its basic meaning is an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The exact force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself remains straightforward: to whistle or make a whistling sound.

This Greek LXX verb means “escape”: to get away from danger, capture, or an opposing force. It describes the act of avoiding being seized or overcome, rather than remaining in a threatened situation. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is consistently that of successfully getting away. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, this verb means “justify.” It describes the act of declaring or treating someone as right rather than condemned. As a verb, it expresses an action, not a person, place, or quality. This LXX word occurs 39 times across 38 verses, in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on that passage’s wording and context.

“Cunning” describes acting with craftiness or deliberate deceit. As a verb, it expresses dealing in a sly, crafty way rather than acting openly. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears twice, both times in Psalms, so its use is focused rather than broad or frequent. Its precise force in either psalm depends on the surrounding verse, but the central idea remains crafty conduct intended to mislead or conceal. The two references are Psalms 14:3 and 35:3.

This Greek LXX verb means “use ill words”—to speak harmfully or abusively against someone. It describes an action expressed through speech rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 7:41. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the precise force of the statement must be understood from that passage’s context.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “weigh down”: to burden, press upon, or make something feel heavy. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its exact force depends on what is being weighed down in the sentence. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Nehemiah and once in Zechariah, showing a limited but consistent use for imposing heaviness or burden. This verb means “put one's hand in.” It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality, so it functions in a sentence as a verb. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in four verses across 2 Chronicles and Jeremiah. The basic idea remains the same wherever it occurs: someone performs the action of putting a hand in. The surrounding verse is needed to determine what that action refers to in a particular passage, but the word itself expresses this direct action.

This noun means “national ruler,” referring to a person who governs a people or nation. It describes a position of public authority rather than a personal quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs three times, all in 1 Maccabees, where the word is used within formal accounts of rulers and political authority. The precise force in any one occurrence depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a ruler over a nation or people.

This word means “anything engraven”—something carved, cut, or shaped into a lasting form. It is a noun describing an engraved object rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 36:13, so its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. The word points to a crafted item marked by engraving, not to a person or an abstract idea.

This Greek LXX noun means “plate,” referring to a flat piece or sheet of material. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Habakkuk 2:19. The basic word identifies a physical object rather than an action, person, or quality. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the ordinary meaning remains a plate or flat sheet.

Eliab, also rendered Eliav, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object; its role is to name particular individuals. This name occurs 28 times in 28 Old Testament verses, beginning in Exodus and continuing through 2 Chronicles. The same name appears in passages from Exodus, Numbers, Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles, identifying people within those historical records.

This adjective describes someone or something as alive, possessing breath and therefore living rather than dead. Its central idea is the presence of life, expressed either by the condition of being alive or by the breath that marks a living creature. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 10 times, chiefly in Joshua, with one occurrence in Deuteronomy. The surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis falls more naturally on living beings or on their breath.

gl: for the sake of; on account of
d: for the sake of; on account of

e.t: This word means “for the sake of” or “on account of.” It points to the purpose, reason, or cause behind an action, event, or decision. As a preposition or adverb, it connects what happens with the person, thing, or circumstance that explains why it happens. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 129 times, so it commonly expresses motives and reasons across many passages. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding words and situation.

This Greek LXX verb means “utterly desolate”: to leave a place or land completely deserted and emptied. It describes thorough devastation rather than a minor loss or temporary inconvenience. The word appears 18 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 17 verses, and is used in passages concerning lands, cities, and places brought into a condition of desolation. As a verb, it expresses the action or result of making something utterly desolate. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “ladder,” referring to a structure used for climbing from one level to another. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 2:31. The word itself gives the ordinary meaning, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain how that ladder functions in the passage. Its sense is concrete and straightforward rather than a broad description of a person, action, or quality.

This noun means “mastery” or “dominion”—the possession or exercise of prevailing control. It identifies authority or power held over someone or something, rather than describing an action by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times, all in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in a sentence depends on what or whom the mastery concerns, but its central idea remains control that prevails.

This noun means “provisions”: supplies prepared or provided for use, especially what people need for a journey or daily support. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times across 11 verses, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, and Psalms. The word therefore refers broadly to material supplies rather than to a person, action, or abstract quality. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Eselon is a proper name, referring to a person or place identified by that name rather than describing an action or quality. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 4:12. The available information preserves the name as “Eselōn” or “Eselon,” but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain more about the individual or location it identifies.

This adjective describes someone who is in “extreme old age,” referring to the very latest or most advanced stage of life. It presents old age as far advanced, rather than simply indicating that a person is older. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Sirach 41:2, so its normal meaning is clear but its wider range of use is limited. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “poorly; meanly,” describing the manner in which something is done. As an adverb, it tells how an action is carried out rather than naming a person, place, or object. Its sense can point to inadequate performance or conduct marked by meanness, while the surrounding sentence determines the precise force. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 15:38.

This is the proper name Isaiah, also represented as “Hēsaΐas” or “Iseas.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, the name occurs 34 times, especially in Isaiah and 2 Kings. Its repeated use across these books marks it as a personal name connected with the biblical figure Isaiah. The name’s precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage.

Thanaemeth is a proper name, presented as the name Thanaemeth rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint text, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 47:8. The available wording preserves the name itself but does not identify from the name alone whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise reference therefore belongs to the surrounding verse and passage.

“Alcoves” refers to recessed spaces or small chambers built into a wall or structure. It is a noun naming these architectural features, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs three times, all in Ezekiel 40:12, 40:14, and 40:16. Its central meaning remains consistent: it identifies designated recessed spaces within the described structure. The precise significance of those alcoves in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage and its description of the building.

This word means “tongs; pliers,” a noun for a hand tool used to grip or handle something. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Kings 7, referring to equipment associated with the temple furnishings. Its basic meaning is therefore a pair of gripping tools, rather than an action or quality. The exact force in either verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies the implement.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Ideadalea” and also given as “Itheathalea.” It identifies a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:39. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, its precise referent cannot be described further, but the word itself functions as a name within that passage.

This proper noun refers to Hierichō, or Jericho, the name of a place. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or person, but a geographical name used to identify the city or region called Jericho in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings. It occurs 62 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages in Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, and later writings. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage.

Iokom is a proper name—the personal name rendered “Iokom” in the Greek Old Testament. It is not an ordinary descriptive word or action; it identifies an individual by name. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 24:23. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide the surrounding verse text, so the person’s identity and role must be established from that passage rather than from the name alone.

This adjective describes someone or something covered in heavy perspiration—sweating profusely. It identifies an outward physical condition rather than an action, emotion, or character trait. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 8:6, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic meaning remains clear: describing intense or abundant sweating. The word therefore helps readers recognize a visible bodily condition expressed in the text.

This Greek LXX verb means “laid up” or “lie down.” It describes someone or something resting in a lying or laid-down position. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related biblical Greek writings represented here: twice in Proverbs and once in Wisdom. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary sense concerns being placed or remaining down rather than standing or moving.

This verb means to condemn: to declare someone guilty, blameworthy, or deserving judgment. It describes an act of judging against a person rather than merely observing wrongdoing. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, appearing in Esther, Daniel, Wisdom, and Susanna. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

“Strike down” is the basic meaning of this Greek LXX verb. It describes an action in which someone or something is brought down by a blow or forceful strike. The word occurs ten times in the Greek LXX corpus, across three Old Testament verses and seven Deuterocanonical verses. It appears in Joshua, Job, and several Maccabees books, showing use across this corpus without changing its central action.

This adjective describes someone or something that is “holding fast”—remaining firmly attached, staying secure, or refusing to let go. It presents steadfast attachment rather than a brief or casual grasp. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Jonah 2:7. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning centers on firmly holding or clinging. The word therefore conveys persistence and stability in whatever relationship or situation the context describes.

This verb means to “crave for strange food.” It describes a strong desire for food that is unusual or different from what is normally eaten, functioning as an action word rather than a name or description of a person. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, at Psalm 50:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is the act of desiring unfamiliar or unusual food.

This noun refers to a nettle, a plant named directly by the word’s definition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Job 31:40. Since no verse text is provided here, the word’s basic meaning is clear, while its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding sentence and context. The word is therefore a straightforward plant name rather than an abstract quality, action, or person.

This word refers to a nettle, a prickly plant. It is a noun naming the plant itself, rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Isaiah 55:13. Because no verse text or surrounding passage is included here, the word’s broader significance in that verse should be understood from its context; its lexical meaning remains the ordinary name of the nettle plant.

This Greek LXX noun refers to something acquired or possessed as property. It can describe an owned possession, land, or other property held by a person or family. The central idea is ownership gained or property belonging to someone, rather than the act of acquiring something viewed by itself. It occurs 37 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, with uses extending from Genesis through Baruch. Its precise sense in a particular verse depends on what possession or acquisition the surrounding passage discusses.

This word means “treacherously.” It describes an action carried out in a treacherous manner, marking the character of what someone does rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 21:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but its basic lexical sense remains an adverbial description of treacherous action.

This Greek LXX adjective means “smooth,” describing something even, sleek, or free from roughness. It can refer to a physical surface, but its ordinary sense may also describe a smooth quality more broadly. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, with most occurrences in Genesis. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being described, but the central idea remains something smooth rather than rough or uneven.

This Greek LXX noun means “speaking-place,” referring to a designated place associated with speaking. In its biblical usage, it is especially connected with the priestly furnishings and worship instructions described in Exodus, though its exact reference in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, appearing most often in Exodus. It is a concrete noun naming a place rather than an action or spoken message.

This verb describes acting in a pestilent or injurious way: it can refer to being harmful or to committing injury. Its basic sense concerns conduct that damages another person, rather than merely naming a condition or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 19:19. The word is a verb, and the verse text is needed to show how this harmful action functions in that particular sentence.

Manna is the name of the food God provided for Israel in the wilderness. As a noun, it refers to that particular provision rather than to food in general. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears 10 times, chiefly in Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Joshua. These passages preserve manna as a remembered part of Israel’s journey: God used it to sustain the people during their wilderness years, and its appearance continued only for the appointed period. The word therefore points to God’s provision of food in Israel’s wilderness experience.

Meida is a proper name, also rendered as “Mitha.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:54. The available information establishes the name and its occurrence, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the person’s role or significance there. Its precise reference in that passage therefore depends on reading the surrounding context.

This adjective describes something as “idle” or “useless”—something lacking productive purpose or practical value. It is a descriptive word rather than a name or action, so its exact force depends on the person or thing being described in the surrounding sentence. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 16:6. The available lexical sense is concise, but it clearly points to something ineffective, unproductive, or without useful result. The passage itself would be needed to explain what particular object or situation the word describes there.

This Greek LXX noun means “mill,” referring to the implement used for grinding. It names a physical object rather than an action or quality. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, across Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, 2 Samuel, and Isaiah. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it appears, while the surrounding verse determines how the mill is being mentioned.

Nabousachar is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name is also rendered Navusakhar, giving two forms for the same named individual. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 46:3. Because the available information identifies the person’s name but does not provide the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish that person’s role or significance in the passage.

Nachem, also rendered Nakhem, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. As a proper noun in the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person by name. It occurs once in this corpus, at 1 Chronicles 4:19. The available information establishes the name’s identification and spelling forms, but does not provide a separate lexical definition or enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person or passage.

This LXX noun means “currency,” referring to money used or considered in an economic setting. It names monetary value rather than a person, action, or quality. The word occurs twice in the LXX corpus: once in Ezra and once in 1 Maccabees. Its precise use in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains currency—money involved in payment, exchange, or financial dealings.

Ommin is a proper name, rendered as “Ommin.” The available lexical information identifies it as a name rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Deuteronomy 2:10–11. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its specific referent cannot be identified further; the secure meaning is the name itself, preserved in English as Ommin.

This adjective describes something as “straight up” or “going upwards.” It points to a direction or position that rises rather than moving sideways or downward. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 28:14. Its basic sense is direct and spatial: something stands or moves upward in a straight direction. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what it describes there, but the word itself expresses upward movement or orientation.

This noun means a small fortification—a place built for protection or defense. It refers to a modest fortified position rather than a person, action, or abstract quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 16:15. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s precise significance in that passage cannot be described further; its central sense remains a small defensive stronghold.

This adjective describes someone or something as “all-depraved” or “thoroughly knavish”—completely corrupt, wicked, or dishonest in character. It is a strong, comprehensive description rather than a mild criticism. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 14:27. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly whom or what it describes there, but the word itself conveys extreme moral badness and knavery.

This word refers to candor: speaking openly, frankly, and without concealment. It can describe the quality of straightforward speech or the manner of speaking candidly. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 12 times across 12 verses, showing a recurring concern with honest, unhindered expression rather than secrecy or evasion. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb means “become dark,” describing a change into a darker condition rather than simply naming darkness itself. It can be used for something that loses brightness or takes on a dark appearance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Lamentations 5:10. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what becomes dark there, but the word’s basic sense remains a movement or change toward darkness.

This word means “wealth” or “treasure,” referring to valuable possessions or riches. It is a noun used for something regarded as a store of value or abundance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Psalms and Ecclesiastes, so its basic sense is consistent but its precise emphasis depends on the surrounding verse. The related English rendering is “treasure,” which closely reflects the idea of accumulated valuable goods.

This adjective means “embroidered” or “related to embroidery,” describing something made with decorative needlework. It belongs to the Greek Old Testament and occurs twice, once in Exodus and once in Job. The word therefore points to crafted, stitched decoration rather than a person, action, or abstract quality. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary sense remains connected with embroidery and embroidered work.

This noun means “battle”—a conflict or fighting between opposing sides. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly for battle as a recognized event or condition, rather than for a person or weapon. It occurs 337 times across 328 verses, showing that warfare is a recurring subject in the translated Scriptures. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This adjective means “rash.” It describes a person, choice, or action that is rash rather than careful and measured. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: twice in Proverbs and once in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains a warning about rashness or impulsive conduct.
